draft.title: Solar and lunar eclipses
card: An eclipse happens when one object in space casts its shadow on another. The sun, Earth and moon must line up almost in a straight line.
The moon passes between the sun and Earth. The moon's shadow falls on part of the Earth, and the sun is blocked from view for people in that shadow.
The Earth is between the sun and the moon. The Earth's shadow falls on the moon, so the moon looks dim and often reddish.
A solar eclipse can only be seen from the part of Earth that the moon's shadow touches. A lunar eclipse can be seen by anyone on the night side of Earth, where the moon is above the horizon.
draft.remember: Solar: the moon blocks the sun. Lunar: Earth's shadow covers the moon.

a.q: During an eclipse, the Earth's shadow falls on the moon. What kind of eclipse is this, and what is the order of the three bodies?
opts: Lunar eclipse, with Earth between the sun and moon
Lunar eclipse, with the moon between the sun and Earth
Solar eclipse, with Earth between the sun and moon
Solar eclipse, with the moon between the sun and Earth
a.why: A lunar eclipse is when the moon is darkened by Earth's shadow, so Earth must sit between the sun and the moon. The last option describes a real arrangement, but it is a solar eclipse, where the moon's shadow falls on Earth.
a.clue: Which object is casting the shadow, and which is receiving it?

b.q: Priya in Perth sees the moon pass in front of the sun and block its light. Her cousin in Darwin sees the sun as normal. What best explains this?
opts: The moon's shadow covers only part of the Earth
The Earth's shadow covers only part of the moon
The moon's shadow covers the whole day side of Earth
The Earth's shadow covers the whole night side of Earth
b.why: This is a solar eclipse, and the moon's shadow is small, so it touches only part of the Earth. Only people in that shadow see the sun blocked. The Earth's shadow is involved in lunar eclipses, not in this case.
b.clue: Think about which shadow is falling on the Earth, and how much of it that shadow covers.

a.best: Lunar eclipse, with Earth between the sun and moon

b.best: The moon's shadow covers only part of the Earth

problems.detail: The why refers to 'the last option', but options are shown in a random order, so students may see a different option in that position and be confused.
